1	# Intake
2	
3	One recipe for every ticket source, plus ad-hoc work with no ticket.
4	
5	## Fetch and preflight
6	
7	| Source | Fetch | ticketId |
8	|---|---|---|
9	| GitHub issue (`#N` / `GH-N`) | none — `intake_preflight` calls `gh` itself | `GH-<N>` |
10	| Jira key (`PROJ-123`) | Atlassian Rovo connector | `PROJ-123` |
11	| ClickUp task (`CU-<id>` or a ClickUp URL) | ClickUp MCP (e.g. `clickup_get_task`) | `CU-<id>` — keeps commits/branches consistent alongside GH-/Jira refs |
12	| Ad-hoc (no ticket) | none — derive title, description, and acceptance criteria from the conversation (the user's message usually already contains them) | any stable id the conversation doesn't already use (e.g. `adhoc-<slug>`) |
13	
14	Call `intake_preflight({source, identifier (github only), ticketId, ticketData (jira/clickup/adhoc), userHint})` — pass `userHint` when the invocation names a mode or pace (e.g. "lite", "quick"), including an explicit "default"/"standard" request. Pass it only with words the user addressed to the workflow's mode or pace itself (for example "do this quick", "lite", "use default mode") — never with the ticket's own title or description text, which routinely contains those same words ("fix the small bug", "by default the button …") without meaning to pick a mode. It creates the ticket's record at INTAKE itself and returns `{ticket, modeResolution, questions[], entry}` — idempotent: calling it again for the same ticket (e.g. a resumed session) returns the existing record's `entry`. The one exception: it refuses a ticket whose stored record is invalid (an error containing `is invalid (`) — take that to SKILL.md's invalid-ticket question. Ad-hoc uses the same call (`source: "adhoc"`, `ticketData: {title, description, acceptanceCriteria, sourceUrl: null, labels: []}` built from the conversation) — it is not a separate, `state_create`-based path; that alias has been removed.
15	
16	## Attachment Check
17	
18	Before scoping, check the fetched issue for attachments and scan its description for evidence keywords ("see attached", "PDF", "screenshot", "evidence") and for embedded image/attachment links (e.g. a markdown image reference `![...](...)`) — a screenshot carries no guarantee a keyword appears near it. The description is a summary — for audit/security tickets, the evidence pinpointing the real code path often lives only in an attachment (real example: CFRVIP-3657, where the description pointed at the wrong leak vector until the attached PDF's figures showed the actual one).
19	
20	- **GitHub:** `intake_preflight` is itself the fetch (no separate pre-fetch step exists), so run this check on its returned `ticket.description` right after that call, before batching `questions` into AskUserQuestion. Also pull the issue's comments (`gh issue view <n> --json comments`) and scan those — the fetch inside `intake_preflight` does not request comments, so evidence posted there is otherwise invisible.
21	- **Jira:** include `attachment` and `comment` in the `fields` of the pre-fetch `getJiraIssue` call (not a separate call) — this check runs on that fetch, before calling `intake_preflight`.
22	- **ClickUp:** read the task's attachments from that same pre-fetch (e.g. via `clickup_get_task`) — this check runs on that fetch, before calling `intake_preflight`.
23	
24	Fetch and read each attachment found before brainstorming. Only auto-fetch attachment references hosted on the ticket's own platform (its attachment API, or an embedded link on that platform's own asset domain) — name any other embedded URL, whether in the description or a comment, as a lead rather than fetching it, since a ticket can be filed by an external or untrusted reporter; fold that into the same batched `AskUserQuestion` call the Questions section already collects, not a separate prompt. If any of these fetches — an attachment, the GitHub comments pull, or a Jira/ClickUp comment field — can't be retrieved, say so rather than silently scoping from the description alone.
25	
26	Record anything an attachment or comment reveals in the ticket's `description`/`acceptanceCriteria`: for Jira/ClickUp, whose check runs before `intake_preflight`, fold it straight into the `ticketData` passed to that call; for GitHub, whose check runs after `intake_preflight` already created the record, fold it into the **Exit to BRANCH** call's fields instead. Either way, PROPOSE (where scoping happens) reads from state, not from this session's memory of the fetch.
27	
28	## Modes
29	
30	**default** — a written plan from `superpowers:writing-plans` (or a short design note when the ticket names the change exactly), executed by `superpowers:subagent-driven-development` with automated review gates and no human-review pause. **lite** — the fast path for trivial work: a one-paragraph plan, direct implementation, a test run, and a PR. No brainstorming, no TDD gate, no reviewer or verifier subagents, no learning-capture. People still review the GitHub PR.
31	
32	`default` is the default mode. Mode applies automatically and is announced, never asked.
33	
34	### The trivial bar
35	
36	A change is **trivial** when both are true:
37	1. It changes no runtime behavior that a test could observe — a version bump, a typo, copy text, docs or comments, a config value the ticket states exactly, a dependency pin.
38	2. The ticket names the change exactly; nothing needs investigating to find what to change.
39	
40	It is **not trivial** when it touches logic, control flow, a function signature, a schema or a data shape; when it is a bug fix (a bug fix needs a test that reproduces it); or when finding the cause or the location needs investigation. Not sure → not trivial.
41	
42	### Picking the mode
43	
44	- **The user asks for lite** (`modeResolution.source` is `userHint` and `mode` is `lite`, or a message addressed to the workflow itself — not the ad-hoc ticket's own title or description text — says lite, quick, trivial, simple, small, express or yolo): `lite`, `modeSource: "user"`. Announce `modeResolution.announce`, and `modeResolution.nudge` if present.
45	- **Otherwise, apply the trivial bar to the ticket.** Clearly trivial → `lite`, `modeSource: "session"`, and announce "Proceeding in lite (trivial: <one-phrase reason>) — say 'default' to switch." Anything else → `default`, `modeSource: null`, and announce `modeResolution.announce`.
46	- An explicit "default"/"standard" request always wins. Labels never pick lite.
47	
48	## Questions
49	
50	Batch every open question into ONE `AskUserQuestion` call (it supports up to 4 questions):
51	- Tracked source: `intake_preflight`'s returned `questions[]`.
52	- Ad-hoc: genuine gaps in title/description/acceptance criteria only — ask nothing if nothing is missing.
53	
54	For a **CFRVIP Jira** ticket with no acceptance criteria, add one `jira-ticket-assist` (Enhance mode) offer to the same batch, noting that it runs a multi-turn interview and approval cycle before it writes to Jira; if taken, run it, re-read the ticket, and `state_update` the criteria. Skip the offer silently for any other source or project, or if that skill isn't installed.
55	
56	## Create state
57	
58	`intake_preflight` already created the record (above), for every source including ad-hoc — nothing further to create here. If a batched question changed `acceptanceCriteria`/`title`/`description` (e.g. a `jira-ticket-assist` Enhance round), fold those into the INTAKE exit call below rather than a separate write.
59	
60	**No acceptance criteria on the ticket?** Derive them from the description and announce them — never block. A bug ticket's description usually *is* the criterion, so stopping to ask would interrupt most intakes. The derived list standing is a valid outcome.
61	
62	**A criterion for every problem the description names.** Whatever supplied the list — the ticket's own declared acceptance criteria, `intake_preflight`'s parsed list, or one this session derived from the description — check it against the *whole* description before moving on, not only its "Expected"/ask section. A sentence naming a second problem (for example, "X has the same issue") gets its own criterion, exactly like the primary ask. A problem leaves scope only when the ticket itself declares it a non-goal, or later, when the user releases it under `review-entry.md`'s two-bar test; deciding on your own that it looks like a follow-up is neither. A non-empty list is not proof this check happened: `intake_preflight`'s parser can return the wrong list outright (for example, the checkbox pass matches anywhere in the body, so a checklist under an unrelated heading like "Definition of Done" can outrank the ticket's own declared AC section) — read the description yourself and compare, every time, regardless of source.
63	
64	**Never omit `acceptanceCriteria`** — the closure check at REVIEW reads it back, and a ticket created without it silently degrades that check.
65	
66	IF you see a ticket reference and think "I'll just start coding" — the ticket MUST go through this recipe first. There is no shortcut that skips state creation.
67	
68	## Exit to BRANCH
69	
70	INTAKE's only exit: `state_update({ticketId, fields: {state: "BRANCH", mode, modeSource, acceptanceCriteria, title?, description?}})` — `mode` and `modeSource` come from **Picking the mode** above. Do this before moving on to `branch.md` — `branch_setup` requires the ticket to already be in BRANCH state (its own exit takes it from there to PROPOSE in one write).
71	
72	## Red flags
73	
74	| Thought | Reality |
75	|---|---|
76	| "Intake needs title/description/AC — I'll ask" | Derive them from the conversation first. Ask only what's genuinely missing, in one batched call. |
77

entries.name: mcp__plugin_pixiepowers_pxs-ops__branch_setup
entries.description: Create or resume a feature branch in one step. Requires the ticket to already be in BRANCH state (state_update({state: "BRANCH"}) is INTAKE's own exit — call it first). Resolves branch name, checks for conflicts, and creates the branch in the current tree (the session's `cwd` — pass it; see the `cwd` parameter) based off the default branch (never current HEAD) or off `baseBranch` when given, performing exactly one state write, BRANCH -> PROPOSE. A session tree that differs from the server's own is recorded for the ticket's later git calls. Returns a question only when the branch already exists. Uncommitted changes are carried onto the new branch when they don't conflict with that base; if they conflict, setup refuses with guidance to commit or stash first. Call again with answers if questions are returned.

branchName.description: Override branch name. If omitted, derived from ticket title.

branchAction.description: How to handle an existing branch. Provide after receiving a branch_exists question, and pass the same `cwd` on the retry.

worktreeDecision.description: Pass 'worktree' ONLY when the user explicitly asked for a worktree. Never propose or ask; omitting it means current tree.

baseBranch.description: Start the new branch from this branch instead of the default branch: origin/<baseBranch> after a best-effort fetch, else local <baseBranch>, else the tool refuses. Applies to the current tree and to a requested worktree, and is recorded so REVIEW diffs only this branch's own commits. Use it for a stacked slice; omit it otherwise. Pass the same value on a retry after a branch_exists question.

cwd.description: The session's current working directory: the path last entered with EnterWorktree if any, else the 'Working directory:' line of <PIXIEPOWERS_CONTEXT>. Omit it when that line is absent or says "withheld". Pass it: the MCP server is long-lived and its own process.cwd() is wherever Claude Code started, which is not where the session is after a worktree switch. The branch is created in this tree, and a session tree that differs from the server's tree is recorded for the ticket (as sessionCwd, not as `worktree`). Pass the same `cwd` on the retry after a branch_exists question.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_pixiepowers_pxs-ops__commit
entries.description: Stage files and create a conventional commit. Builds message as: <type>(<scope>): <description> [<ticketId>]. Pass 'type' and 'description' as separate params — do NOT pass a combined message string. Pass 'ticketId' so the commit runs in the ticket's worktree (if any) and gets the [ticketId] suffix.

files.description: Array of file paths to git-add before committing

description.description: Commit description — the short text after 'type(scope): '

ticketId.description: Ticket ID appended as [ticketId] and used to resolve the ticket's worktree as the commit cwd (e.g. 'GH-131', 'CFRVIP-2799')

entries.name: mcp__plugin_pixiepowers_pxs-ops__intake_preflight
entries.description: Fetch a ticket, suggest a workflow mode, and create its state.json record at INTAKE (returning `entry`) — idempotent: an existing record's entry is returned unchanged, never an error, and no ticket is ever observed without a record between intake and branch setup. For GitHub: pass source='github' and identifier (issue number). For Jira/ClickUp/external: pass source='jira' or 'clickup' and ticketData with pre-fetched ticket content. Returns mode recommendation and AskUserQuestion-ready questions.

source.description: 'github' fetches via gh CLI; 'jira'/'clickup'/'adhoc' require ticketData

identifier.description: GitHub issue number (e.g. '131'). Required when source='github'.

ticketData.description: Pre-fetched ticket data. Required when source='jira', 'clickup', or 'adhoc'. Not needed for source='github'.

userHint.description: The user's invocation phrasing when it names a workflow mode or pace (e.g. 'lite', 'quick fix', 'yolo', or an explicit 'default'/'standard' request). Mode resolves to default unless this signals lite; labels never pick lite.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_pixiepowers_pxs-ops__pr_create
entries.description: Push branch to origin and create a pull request. Pass 'branch' (feature branch), 'title', 'body', and optionally 'baseBranch' (target branch like 'main' or 'dev'). When 'ticketId' is passed and the ticket records a branch, 'branch' must equal it; otherwise the call is refused. The PR is assigned to the workflow driver by default; pass 'assignees' to override (empty array = no assignees). Pass 'attachments' to upload screenshots; the PR is never blocked by them.

branch.description: Feature branch name to push (e.g. 'keki/GH-131-my-feature'). With 'ticketId', must equal the ticket's recorded branch.

baseBranch.description: Target/base branch for the PR (e.g. 'main', 'dev'). Defaults to repo default branch if omitted.

ticketId.description: Ticket ID — if provided, updates ticket state with the PR URL

assignees.description: GitHub usernames to assign to the PR. Defaults to the workflow driver (session username) when omitted; pass an empty array to assign no one.

attachments.description: Files to upload with gh --attach (gh 2.99.0+, GitHub.com only). gh appends each file to the end of the body; do not reference them in the body. A missing file, a relative path or a path containing '#' is rejected; an old gh, an Enterprise Server host or a failed first upload creates the PR without them and returns attachmentsSkipped; a partial upload returns attachmentWarning.

path.description: Absolute path to an existing image or video file, e.g. a screenshot in the session scratchpad.

alt.description: Alt text for the image. `gh` uses it only for an appended file; a file the body references keeps the alt text written in the Markdown.

refresh.description: Force re-resolve cached metadata (username, defaultBranch). Default: false.

1	# Branch
2	
3	Call `branch_setup({ticketId})` once intake is confirmed and the ticket is in BRANCH state (`intake.md`'s own exit gets it there) — `branch_setup` refuses otherwise. The default is the current tree — which may itself be a worktree created by external tooling (e.g. Superset); stay in it. Pass `cwd` — the session's current working directory: the path last entered with `EnterWorktree` if any, else the `Working directory:` line of `<PIXIEPOWERS_CONTEXT>` — so the branch lands in the session's tree even when the MCP server started elsewhere. Omit `cwd` when that line is absent or says "withheld". Do not ask about or propose a worktree on your own.
4	
5	Pass `worktreeDecision: "worktree"` when the user asks for one in-the-moment **OR has a standing preference for worktrees** — a preference stated in their project instructions (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), a remembered preference, or one they've expressed before (common when the user runs multiple concurrent sessions against a single checkout, where a shared tree lets one session's `git checkout` land another's commits on the wrong branch). A standing preference counts as the explicit request and should be honored by default, without re-asking. Absent any such signal, keep the current-tree default.
6	
7	If `branch_setup` returns `needsInput: true`, pipe ONLY the returned `questions` array to `AskUserQuestion` — do NOT invent additional prompts. The branch name is auto-derived and returned in `branchName`; surface it only if a returned question requires it. Call `branch_setup` again with the same `cwd` and the answers: `branchAction` for a `branch_exists` question, and `branchName` ONLY when the user picked "Different name".
8	
9	When the user requested a worktree, `branch_setup` runs `git worktree add` and returns `{ branch, worktree, needsTool: "EnterWorktree", enterWorktreePath }` — invoke `EnterWorktree({ path: enterWorktreePath })` before continuing. This moves the session's working directory into the worktree so plain Bash, Read/Edit/Write, and Grep all operate on the right tree without explicit `cd`. Requires the harness `worktree.baseRef: fresh` setting (default).
10	
11	`branch_setup` advances the ticket to PROPOSE itself — do NOT call `state_update` here. Continue with `propose.md`.
12

# Branch

Call `branch_setup({ticketId})` once intake is confirmed and the ticket is in BRANCH state (`intake.md`'s own exit gets it there) — `branch_setup` refuses otherwise. The default is the current tree — which may itself be a worktree created by external tooling (e.g. Superset); stay in it. Pass `cwd` — the session's current working directory: the path last entered with `EnterWorktree` if any, else the `Working directory:` line of `<PIXIEPOWERS_CONTEXT>` — so the branch lands in the session's tree even when the MCP server started elsewhere. Omit `cwd` when that line is absent or says "withheld". Do not ask about or propose a worktree on your own.

Pass `worktreeDecision: "worktree"` when the user asks for one in-the-moment **OR has a standing preference for worktrees** — a preference stated in their project instructions (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), a remembered preference, or one they've expressed before (common when the user runs multiple concurrent sessions against a single checkout, where a shared tree lets one session's `git checkout` land another's commits on the wrong branch). A standing preference counts as the explicit request and should be honored by default, without re-asking. Absent any such signal, keep the current-tree default.

If `branch_setup` returns `needsInput: true`, pipe ONLY the returned `questions` array to `AskUserQuestion` — do NOT invent additional prompts. The branch name is auto-derived and returned in `branchName`; surface it only if a returned question requires it. Call `branch_setup` again with the same `cwd` and the answers: `branchAction` for a `branch_exists` question, and `branchName` ONLY when the user picked "Different name".

When the user requested a worktree, `branch_setup` runs `git worktree add` and returns `{ branch, worktree, needsTool: "EnterWorktree", enterWorktreePath }` — invoke `EnterWorktree({ path: enterWorktreePath })` before continuing. This moves the session's working directory into the worktree so plain Bash, Read/Edit/Write, and Grep all operate on the right tree without explicit `cd`. Requires the harness `worktree.baseRef: fresh` setting (default).

`branch_setup` advances the ticket to PROPOSE itself — do NOT call `state_update` here. Continue with `propose.md`.

acceptanceCriteria: Every documented config/env var, route, behavior and deploy step is checked against the code
Each discrepancy found is fixed (docs updated to match code, or code fixed where the doc states the intended behavior and the code is clearly a bug)
The PR lists each discrepancy and how it was reconciled
Tests pass

2	
3	The ticket's mode picks the section: **Default** or **Lite**.
4	
5	## Default
6	
7	Invoke `superpowers:brainstorming` via the Skill tool for every default ticket. Tell it this ticket ships code — it is never a spike.
8	
9	### No approval stop
10	
11	Tell brainstorming to present the design and **continue without waiting for approval** — on both its bounded and architectural paths. This deliberately overrides brainstorming's own HARD-GATE: the goal of both modes is no human stop between intake and PR. The user can still interrupt at any time.
12	
13	The same override covers every other wait brainstorming builds in: no approval after each design section, no wait for the user to review the written spec, no visual-companion offer. It also covers the wait `superpowers:writing-plans` builds in for the user to review the saved plan (see **The plan document**).
14	
15	Clarifying questions are answered by the session, not the user, wherever the ticket, the codebase, or your own best judgment can settle them — record the answer in the design itself. Collect only the questions that genuinely need the user — a decision the ticket and codebase cannot settle — and ask them all at once, in a single `AskUserQuestion` call; never one at a time. Hold any question that needs the user until brainstorming's bounded/architectural call is made.
16	
17	If brainstorming wrote a spec file, do not commit it here — PROPOSE cannot commit. It lands in the first APPLY commit.
18	
19	At most one stop happens at PROPOSE: the single batched `AskUserQuestion` call above.
20	
21	### The plan document
22	
23	After the design is presented, decide whether the ticket needs a plan document. **Skip it** only when both hold:
24	
25	1. The ticket names the change exactly — `intake.md`'s trivial bar, second clause: nothing needs investigating to find what to change. The naming sentence must be in the ticket's own text, not in acceptance criteria intake derived.
26	2. Your design makes no choice the ticket leaves open. Tests that prove the ticket's stated behavior are not a choice, because TDD adds them on every ticket. A new interface, a new production file or module, a second viable approach, or behavior the ticket does not state is a choice.
27	
28	Anything else — including not sure — gets the plan. Invoke `superpowers:writing-plans` via the Skill tool, even when brainstorming classified the ticket bounded. This overrides brainstorming's own terminal-state routing for the plan-document decision only.
29	
30	**Plan path.** Tell `writing-plans` to save the plan to `entry.planPath` — the state directory, not the repo. Plans are never committed.
31	
32	**Skip path.** Do not invoke `writing-plans`. Write a design note to `entry.planPath` instead, with an `Outcomes` list (the closure check reads it) and each task's files and test-first steps — the subagent-driven implementer sees only its own task. State in the note's first line which ticket sentence names the change exactly.
33	
34	**Both paths.** Record `entry.planPath` in the ticket's `plan` field via `state_update`. On the plan path, skip `writing-plans`' whole Execution Handoff section, in both of its forms — the "Which approach?" question and the "Please review the plan" wait — and do not wait for a plan review. Default always executes with `superpowers:subagent-driven-development` (see `apply.md`), so a skipped plan still gets the per-task and whole-branch reviews. Continue to PROPOSE's exit as soon as the plan or note is saved and self-reviewed. If `entry.planPath` is absent (the ticket id isn't a safe file name), skip the file and record the plan or note inline on the `plan` field instead.
35	
36	## Lite
37	
38	No brainstorming. Write a one-paragraph plan: what changes, in which files, and how the tests show it works. Then check the change against the trivial bar in `intake.md`.
39	
40	- **Passes the bar** → record the paragraph on `plan` and exit to APPLY.
41	- **Fails the bar, `modeSource: "session"`** → escalate. Tell the user in one line: "Moving to default: <reason>." Then `state_update({ticketId, fields: {mode: "default", modeSource: null}})` and follow **Default** above without waiting. Put the same line in the plan's or design note's header (after the note's first line on the skip path), so the PR body repeats it — or, when `entry.planPath` is absent, append it to the `plan` field instead.
42	- **Fails the bar, `modeSource: "user"`** → the user owns the choice. Print one line: "This changes behavior; lite ships it with no new tests or review — say 'default' to switch." Add the same line at the end of the `plan` paragraph, so REVIEW repeats it in the PR body. Continue in lite.
43	
44	If the user asks for lite at PROPOSE, set `mode: "lite", modeSource: "user"` in the same `state_update`.
45	
46	A lite ticket with no `modeSource` is treated as `"session"`.
47	
48	## Both modes
49	
50	Do not invoke `superpowers:dispatching-parallel-agents` here. It is a pattern for debugging several unrelated failures, not a planning step.
51	
52	PROPOSE's exit to APPLY is `state_update({ticketId, fields: {state: "APPLY", plan}})`, and the server refuses it when `plan` is empty — in either mode. Recording nothing here means lost context on session resume: on resume at APPLY or later, read `plan` back to restore context (a plan or design-note path for default, the paragraph itself for lite); if it's empty, re-brainstorm from `acceptanceCriteria`.
53	
54	## Mode changes
55	
56	Changing mode is allowed from PROPOSE. After that, the only change is a lite ticket moving to default from APPLY — session-picked when the change fails the trivial bar, user-picked when the user says "default" (see `apply.md`). From REVIEW on, the mode is locked.
57

59	
60	| Thought | Reality |
61	|---|---|
62	| "I already know what to do, skip brainstorming" | Brainstorming validates your assumption. 30 seconds. Do it. |
63	| "I should wait for the user to approve the design" | Neither mode stops here. Present the design and continue; the user can interrupt. |

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

# drop

A public "send me files" page. Anyone can drag files onto it; nobody but the
owner can get them back out.

- Drag-and-drop upload ([Uppy](https://uppy.io)) over [tus](https://tus.io): 50 MB
  chunks, automatic retries, resume after a dropped connection or a reloaded tab.
- The uploader gets nothing back: no list, no links, no delete.
- When a send finishes, the owner gets an email with a link to a private page for
  that send: download each file or all of them as a .zip, then delete them from the
  server.
- The link is the only credential (a random 192-bit token). There is no login.
- The owner can also make **share links**: download-only, no delete, no sender
  details, expiring after 1, 7 or 30 days, revocable from the owner page.

## Screenshots

The data below is made up: names, links and addresses are examples.

**The upload page**, as anyone sees it, with three files queued:

![Upload page with three files queued](docs/screenshots/upload.png)

**Home mode, after an upload:** one box with the result and a share link ready to
copy or send.

![Finished upload in home mode with a share link](docs/screenshots/home-share.png)

**What the recipient gets:** the files and nothing else.

![Share page with two files to download](docs/screenshots/share.png)

**The owner page:** downloads, share links with their state, and delete.

![Owner page with files, a share link and the delete box](docs/screenshots/owner.png)

**The admin page** (home mode only): disk use, 90-day statistics, inbox, outbox
and history.

![Admin page with disk meter, statistics, inbox, outbox and history](docs/screenshots/admin.png)

## Home mode

A visitor coming from the server's own public address is taken to be the owner at
home (or on a VPN that exits there). For them the banner reads `HOME MODE`, and when
an upload finishes the page offers a share link right away, with Copy and the
system share sheet, so sending something to someone needs no email round trip.
Home-mode uploads send no email; the finish screen links to their owner page
instead. Their files are deleted once their share links run out (links revoked by
hand don't count; with all of them revoked, the files stay), or a day after upload
if no link was ever made.

Expiry needs no extra machinery: a share link is checked against its expiry on
every request, so it stops working on the second. The files go on the app's own
5-minute cleanup pass, the same one that sends late emails and removes abandoned
partial uploads.

The server learns its public address by asking `HOME_LOOKUP_URL` (default
`https://1.1.1.1/cdn-cgi/trace`, which answers with an `ip=` line) and compares it
with Cloudflare's `CF-Connecting-IP`. There is no background polling: a matching
visitor costs nothing, and a mismatch triggers a fresh lookup at most once per
`HOME_RECHECK_SECONDS` (60), so a changed home address is picked up on its own.
A failed lookup keeps the last known address; with none known, nobody is home.
Set `HOME_LOOKUP_URL=` (empty) to turn home mode off.

Home mode also links to `/admin`: disk use against the quota, 90-day statistics
(sends received and downloaded, sends shared and fetched by their recipients, links
made and used), uploads in flight, the inbox (sends to you, with their owner pages),
the outbox (your shares, their links and whether they were fetched), and the
history of deleted sends with why they went. Anyone behind the home address can
open it; from anywhere else `/admin` is a plain 404.

## Guards

Because the page is open to anyone, the app protects the disk it writes to:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MAX_FILE_SIZE` | `50G` | Largest single file |
| `MAX_TOTAL` | `500G` | Everything stored, including uploads in progress |
| `MIN_FREE` | `300G` | Refuse any upload that would leave less than this free on the volume |

Space is reserved at the moment an upload is *created*, from its declared length,
so several concurrent uploads cannot jointly overrun the limits. When an upload is
refused for space, the owner is emailed (at most twice a day).

`DATA_DIR` must contain a `.drop-volume` marker file. If the volume is not mounted,
the marker is missing, so the app refuses uploads and `/healthz` returns 503,
rather than filling the disk underneath the mount point.

Also: 30 new sends and 500 new files per hour per client IP (`CF-Connecting-IP`),
at most 200 files per send. Partial uploads that are not resumed within 7 days are
removed.

## Notifications

The email goes out through an [Apprise API](https://github.com/caronc/apprise-api)
server: `APPRISE_URL` is its `/notify/<key>` endpoint, and `APPRISE_TAG` selects the
target (default `email`). Without `APPRISE_URL`, notifications are only logged.

A send is announced when the uploader's page reports it finished. If the page never
does (the tab was closed), it is announced after 30 quiet minutes
(`IDLE_NOTIFY_MINUTES`). If more files arrive later, another email follows.

## Sender location

Next to the sender's address, the owner page, the admin page and the email show
where it is, for example `86.59.163.158 (Budapest, Hungary)`. The location comes
from Cloudflare's headers on the request that starts the send, and is stored with
it. Nothing is looked up afterwards, and no address goes to a third party.
`CF-IPCountry` is on by default. For city and region, turn on the managed transform
**Add visitor location headers** (Rules → Settings in the zone). Without it only
the country shows. Sends from before this feature show the address alone.

## Running

```bash
npm ci
mkdir -p data && touch data/.drop-volume
DATA_DIR=./data PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:3000 npm start
npm test
```

## Deploying

drop must be reached **only through Cloudflare**. Home mode and the per-IP limits
both read the `CF-Connecting-IP` header; exposed any other way, anyone could set it.
Two ways to run it:

### On its own: `examples/standalone/`

drop, a [Cloudflare Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/connections/connect-networks/)
and an [Apprise API](https://github.com/caronc/apprise-api) server for the emails,
with nothing published on the host. This is an untested starting point:

```bash
cd examples/standalone
cp .env.example .env                                  # PUBLIC_URL, TUNNEL_TOKEN, limits
cp apprise/apprise.yml.example apprise/apprise.yml    # where the emails go
docker compose up -d --build
```

Outside the compose file, in the Cloudflare dashboard: give the tunnel a public
hostname matching `PUBLIC_URL`, with service `http://drop:3000`. Data lives in the
`drop-data` volume; a one-shot `drop-init` container hands it to uid 1000 and adds
the `.drop-volume` marker.

### Behind an existing reverse proxy: `compose.yaml`

The top-level `compose.yaml` is the one in production. It joins the proxy's Docker
network (`DROP_NETWORK`) and stores data at an absolute host path (`DROP_DATA_DIR`).
The proxy must pass `CF-Connecting-IP` through, allow request bodies over 50 MB,
and stream rather than buffer. For nginx:

```nginx
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name drop.example.com;

    client_max_body_size 60M;              # tus sends 50 MB chunks

    resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off;  # Docker DNS: follow a recreated container
    set $drop http://drop:3000;

    location / {
        proxy_pass $drop;
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
        proxy_set_header CF-Connecting-IP  $http_cf_connecting_ip;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_request_buffering off;       # uploads resume from the last byte that arrived
        proxy_buffering off;               # big downloads and zips stream
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
    }
}
```

### Optional: a Cloudflare rate limit

The app limits sends and files per IP per hour. A Cloudflare rate-limiting rule
stops bursts before they reach it: count only the requests that *create* something,
not the chunk uploads or downloads. For example, 20 requests per 10 seconds per IP,
blocking for 10 seconds:

```
(http.host eq "drop.example.com" and http.request.method eq "POST"
 and http.request.uri.path in {"/files" "/files/" "/api/batches"})
```

Uppy treats the resulting 429 as a rate limit and backs off, so a big send slows
down rather than fails.

## Storage layout

```
DATA_DIR/
  .drop-volume          marker; required
  uploads/<id>          file contents (tus FileStore)
  uploads/<id>.json     tus metadata: size, filename, batch
  batches/<batch>.json  one per send: owner token, file list, share links, notification state
```

## License

[MIT](LICENSE): free for anyone to use, modify and redistribute, as long as the
copyright notice stays with every copy.

5	function bytes(name, fallback) {
6	  const raw = process.env[name];
7	  if (!raw) return fallback;
8	  const m = /^(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*([KMGT]?)B?$/i.exec(raw.trim());
9	  if (!m) throw new Error(`${name}: cannot parse "${raw}" as a size (e.g. 10G)`);
10	  const unit = { '': 1, K: 1024, M: 1024 ** 2, G: GB, T: 1024 ** 4 }[m[2].toUpperCase()];
11	  return Math.floor(Number(m[1]) * unit);

# Runs behind a reverse proxy on an existing Docker network. Everything
# deployment-specific (data directory, network, URLs) comes from the environment
# the stack is deployed with; nothing host-specific lives here.
services:
  drop:
    build: .
    image: drop:local
    container_name: drop
    restart: unless-stopped
    # No published port: the reverse proxy reaches the app over a shared network,
    # so nothing can bypass it (and spoof CF-Connecting-IP).
    networks:
      - frontend
    environment:
      - TZ=Europe/Budapest
      - PUBLIC_URL=${PUBLIC_URL:?set PUBLIC_URL}
      - APPRISE_URL=${APPRISE_URL:-}
      - APPRISE_TAG=${APPRISE_TAG:-email}
      - MAX_FILE_SIZE=${MAX_FILE_SIZE:-50G}
      - MAX_TOTAL=${MAX_TOTAL:-500G}
      - MIN_FREE=${MIN_FREE:-300G}
    volumes:
      # Absolute host path, writable by uid 1000 (the image's `node` user), with a
      # `.drop-volume` marker file at its root.
      - ${DROP_DATA_DIR:?set DROP_DATA_DIR}:/data
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    cap_drop:
      - ALL

networks:
  frontend:
    # The reverse proxy's network; created by the proxy's own stack.

# drop on its own: the app, a Cloudflare Tunnel to reach it, and an Apprise API
# server for the emails. Nothing is published on the host; the tunnel is the only
# way in. Copy .env.example to .env and apprise/apprise.yml.example to
# apprise/apprise.yml, fill both in, then `docker compose up -d --build`.
#
# Not tested as a whole: a starting point, not a recipe. The repo's top-level
# compose.yaml is the one in production, behind an existing reverse proxy.
services:
  drop:
    build: ../..
    image: drop:local
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - TZ=${TZ:-UTC}
      - PUBLIC_URL=${PUBLIC_URL:?set PUBLIC_URL}
      - APPRISE_URL=http://apprise:8000/notify/apprise
      - APPRISE_TAG=email
      - MAX_FILE_SIZE=${MAX_FILE_SIZE:-10G}
      - MAX_TOTAL=${MAX_TOTAL:-100G}
      - MIN_FREE=${MIN_FREE:-20G}
    volumes:
      - drop-data:/data
    depends_on:
      drop-init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    cap_drop:
      - ALL

  # A fresh named volume is root-owned and empty. Hand it to the image's `node`
  # user (uid 1000) and add the marker drop insists on before it writes anything.
  drop-init:
    image: busybox:1.37
    command: sh -c 'chown 1000:1000 /data && touch /data/.drop-volume && chown 1000:1000 /data/.drop-volume'
    volumes:
      - drop-data:/data
    restart: "no"

  # In the Cloudflare dashboard, give the tunnel a public hostname (the host in
  # PUBLIC_URL) with service http://drop:3000. Going through Cloudflare is not
  # optional: home mode and the per-IP limits read CF-Connecting-IP.
  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run
    environment:
      - TUNNEL_TOKEN=REDACTED TUNNEL_TOKEN}
    depends_on:
      - drop

  # Stateful "simple" mode: apprise/apprise.yml is the config for the key
  # `apprise`, which is the /notify/apprise in drop's APPRISE_URL.
  apprise:
    image: caronc/apprise:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - TZ=${TZ:-UTC}
      - APPRISE_STATEFUL_MODE=simple
      - APPRISE_WORKER_COUNT=1
    volumes:
      - ./apprise:/config

volumes:
  drop-data:

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM node:24-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts
COPY . .
# A failing test fails the build, so a broken commit never replaces a working container.
RUN npm test && npm prune --omit=dev
# The commit this image is built from, for the version on the pages. Komodo builds
# from a full git clone, so .git is in the context; it stays in this stage.
RUN apk add --no-cache git \
 && git config --global --add safe.directory /app \
 && (git rev-parse HEAD > BUILD || echo dev > BUILD) \
 && rm -rf .git

FROM node:24-alpine
RUN apk add --no-cache tzdata
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 DATA_DIR=/data
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/BUILD ./BUILD
COPY package.json ./
COPY src ./src
COPY public ./public
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s --start-period=10s \
  CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz || exit 1
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

content.content:
1	# drop
2	
3	A public "send me files" page. Anyone can drag files onto it; nobody but the
4	owner can get them back out.
5	
6	- Drag-and-drop upload ([Uppy](https://uppy.io)) over [tus](https://tus.io): 50 MB
7	  chunks, automatic retries, resume after a dropped connection or a reloaded tab.
8	- The uploader gets nothing back: no list, no links, no delete.
9	- When a send finishes, the owner gets an email with a link to a private page for
10	  that send: download each file or all of them as a .zip, then delete them from the
11	  server.
12	- The link is the only credential (a random 192-bit token). There is no login.
13	- The owner can also make **share links**: download-only, no delete, no sender
14	  details, expiring after 1, 7 or 30 days, revocable from the owner page.
15	
16	## Screenshots
17	
18	The data below is made up: names, links and addresses are examples.
19	
20	**The upload page**, as anyone sees it, with three files queued:
21	
22	![Upload page with three files queued](docs/screenshots/upload.png)
23	
24	**Home mode, after an upload:** one box with the result and a share link ready to
25	copy or send.
26	
27	![Finished upload in home mode with a share link](docs/screenshots/home-share.png)
28	
29	**What the recipient gets:** the files and nothing else.
30	
31	![Share page with two files to download](docs/screenshots/share.png)
32	
33	**The owner page:** downloads, share links with their state, and delete.
34	
35	![Owner page with files, a share link and the delete box](docs/screenshots/owner.png)
36	
37	**The admin page** (home mode only): disk use, 90-day statistics, inbox, outbox
38	and history.
39	
40	![Admin page with disk meter, statistics, inbox, outbox and history](docs/screenshots/admin.png)
41	
42	## Home mode
43	
44	A visitor coming from the server's own public address is taken to be the owner at
45	home (or on a VPN that exits there). For them the banner reads `HOME MODE`, and when
46	an upload finishes the page offers a share link right away, with Copy and the
47	system share sheet, so sending something to someone needs no email round trip.
48	Home-mode uploads send no email; the finish screen links to their owner page
49	instead. Their files are deleted once their share links run out (links revoked by
50	hand don't count; with all of them revoked, the files stay), or a day after upload
51	if no link was ever made.
52	
53	Expiry needs no extra machinery: a share link is checked against its expiry on
54	every request, so it stops working on the second. The files go on the app's own
55	5-minute cleanup pass, the same one that sends late emails and removes abandoned
56	partial uploads.
57	
58	The server learns its public address by asking `HOME_LOOKUP_URL` (default
59	`https://1.1.1.1/cdn-cgi/trace`, which answers with an `ip=` line) and compares it
60	with Cloudflare's `CF-Connecting-IP`. There is no background polling: a matching
61	visitor costs nothing, and a mismatch triggers a fresh lookup at most once per
62	`HOME_RECHECK_SECONDS` (60), so a changed home address is picked up on its own.
63	A failed lookup keeps the last known address; with none known, nobody is home.
64	Set `HOME_LOOKUP_URL=` (empty) to turn home mode off.
65	
66	Home mode also links to `/admin`: disk use against the quota, 90-day statistics
67	(sends received and downloaded, sends shared and fetched by their recipients, links
68	made and used), uploads in flight, the inbox (sends to you, with their owner pages),
69	the outbox (your shares, their links and whether they were fetched), and the
70	history of deleted sends with why they went. Anyone behind the home address can
71	open it; from anywhere else `/admin` is a plain 404.
72	
73	## Guards
74	
75	Because the page is open to anyone, the app protects the disk it writes to:
76	
77	| Setting | Default | Meaning |
78	|---|---|---|
79	| `MAX_FILE_SIZE` | `50G` | Largest single file |
80	| `MAX_TOTAL` | `500G` | Everything stored, including uploads in progress |
81	| `MIN_FREE` | `300G` | Refuse any upload that would leave less than this free on the volume |
82	
83	Space is reserved at the moment an upload is *created*, from its declared length,
84	so several concurrent uploads cannot jointly overrun the limits. When an upload is
85	refused for space, the owner is emailed (at most twice a day).
86	
87	`DATA_DIR` must contain a `.drop-volume` marker file. If the volume is not mounted,
88	the marker is missing, so the app refuses uploads and `/healthz` returns 503,
89	rather than filling the disk underneath the mount point.
90	
91	Also: 30 new sends and 500 new files per hour per client IP (`CF-Connecting-IP`),
92	at most 200 files per send. Partial uploads that are not resumed within 7 days are
93	removed.
94	
95	## Notifications
96	
97	The email goes out through an [Apprise API](https://github.com/caronc/apprise-api)
98	server: `APPRISE_URL` is its `/notify/<key>` endpoint, and `APPRISE_TAG` selects the
99	target (default `email`). Without `APPRISE_URL`, notifications are only logged.
100	
101	A send is announced when the uploader's page reports it finished. If the page never
102	does (the tab was closed), it is announced after 30 quiet minutes
103	(`IDLE_NOTIFY_MINUTES`). If more files arrive later, another email follows.
104	
105	## Sender location
106	
107	Next to the sender's address, the owner page, the admin page and the email show
108	where it is, for example `86.59.163.158 (Budapest, Hungary)`. The location comes
109	from Cloudflare's headers on the request that starts the send, and is stored with
110	it. Nothing is looked up afterwards, and no address goes to a third party.
111	`CF-IPCountry` is on by default. For city and region, turn on the managed transform
112	**Add visitor location headers** (Rules → Settings in the zone). Without it only
113	the country shows. Sends from before this feature show the address alone.
114	
115	## Running
116	
117	```bash
118	npm ci
119	mkdir -p data && touch data/.drop-volume
120	DATA_DIR=./data PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:3000 npm start
121	npm test
122	```
123	
124	## Deploying
125	
126	drop must be reached **only through Cloudflare**. Home mode and the per-IP limits
127	both read the `CF-Connecting-IP` header; exposed any other way, anyone could set it.
128	Two ways to run it:
129	
130	### On its own: `examples/standalone/`
131	
132	drop, a [Cloudflare Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/connections/connect-networks/)
133	and an [Apprise API](https://github.com/caronc/apprise-api) server for the emails,
134	with nothing published on the host. This is an untested starting point:
135	
136	```bash
137	cd examples/standalone
138	cp .env.example .env                                  # PUBLIC_URL, TUNNEL_TOKEN, limits
139	cp apprise/apprise.yml.example apprise/apprise.yml    # where the emails go
140	docker compose up -d --build
141	```
142	
143	Outside the compose file, in the Cloudflare dashboard: give the tunnel a public
144	hostname matching `PUBLIC_URL`, with service `http://drop:3000`. Data lives in the
145	`drop-data` volume; a one-shot `drop-init` container hands it to uid 1000 and adds
146	the `.drop-volume` marker.
147	
148	### Behind an existing reverse proxy: `compose.yaml`
149	
150	The top-level `compose.yaml` is the one in production. It joins the proxy's Docker
151	network (`DROP_NETWORK`) and stores data at an absolute host path (`DROP_DATA_DIR`).
152	The proxy must pass `CF-Connecting-IP` through, allow request bodies over 50 MB,
153	and stream rather than buffer. For nginx:
154	
155	```nginx
156	server {
157	    listen 80;
158	    server_name drop.example.com;
159	
160	    client_max_body_size 60M;              # tus sends 50 MB chunks
161	
162	    resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off;  # Docker DNS: follow a recreated container
163	    set $drop http://drop:3000;
164	
165	    location / {
166	        proxy_pass $drop;
167	        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
168	        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
169	        proxy_set_header CF-Connecting-IP  $http_cf_connecting_ip;
170	        proxy_http_version 1.1;
171	        proxy_request_buffering off;       # uploads resume from the last byte that arrived
172	        proxy_buffering off;               # big downloads and zips stream
173	        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
174	        proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
175	    }
176	}
177	```
178	
179	### Optional: a Cloudflare rate limit
180	
181	The app limits sends and files per IP per hour. A Cloudflare rate-limiting rule
182	stops bursts before they reach it: count only the requests that *create* something,
183	not the chunk uploads or downloads. For example, 20 requests per 10 seconds per IP,
184	blocking for 10 seconds:
185	
186	```
187	(http.host eq "drop.example.com" and http.request.method eq "POST"
188	 and http.request.uri.path in {"/files" "/files/" "/api/batches"})
189	```
190	
191	Uppy treats the resulting 429 as a rate limit and backs off, so a big send slows
192	down rather than fails.
193	
194	## Storage layout
195	
196	```
197	DATA_DIR/
198	  .drop-volume          marker; required
199	  uploads/<id>          file contents (tus FileStore)
200	  uploads/<id>.json     tus metadata: size, filename, batch
201	  batches/<batch>.json  one per send: owner token, file list, share links, notification state
202	```
203	
204	## License
205	
206	[MIT](LICENSE): free for anyone to use, modify and redistribute, as long as the
207	copyright notice stays with every copy.
208

4	
5	function bytes(name, fallback) {
6	  const raw = process.env[name];
7	  if (!raw) return fallback;
8	  const m = /^(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*([KMGT]?)B?$/i.exec(raw.trim());
9	  if (!m) throw new Error(`${name}: cannot parse "${raw}" as a size (e.g. 10G)`);
10	  const unit = { '': 1, K: 1024, M: 1024 ** 2, G: GB, T: 1024 ** 4 }[m[2].toUpperCase()];
11	  return Math.floor(Number(m[1]) * unit);
12	}

15

20	  batchesDir: path.join(dataDir, 'batches'),
21	  // A file that must exist in DATA_DIR. If the volume behind it is not mounted, the
22	  // marker is missing and the app refuses uploads instead of filling whatever disk
23	  // happens to sit under the mount point.

25	  requireMarker: process.env.REQUIRE_MARKER !== '0',
26	  publicUrl: (process.env.PUBLIC_URL || '').replace(/\/+$/, ''),
27	  appriseUrl: process.env.APPRISE_URL || '',
28	  appriseTag: process.env.APPRISE_TAG || 'email',
29	  maxFileSize: bytes('MAX_FILE_SIZE', 50 * GB),
30	  // Upper bound for everything stored here, finished or in flight.
31	  maxTotal: bytes('MAX_TOTAL', 500 * GB),
32	  // Uploads are refused if accepting one would leave less than this free on the volume.
33	  minFree: bytes('MIN_FREE', 300 * GB),
34	  maxFilesPerBatch: Number(process.env.MAX_FILES_PER_BATCH || 200),
35	  // A batch whose uploader never pressed "done" (closed the tab) is announced after

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

**vs. Executing Plans (inline):**
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution) instead of one context doing every task
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality) instead of only at the end
- Costs a fresh context per task and per review; inline costs one context plus one final reviewer
- Both run in this session, share the same plan workspace and ledger, and never pause between tasks
